section.title: Gaius Commended for Hospitality
section.sectionRationale: The letter turns from praise of Gaius the man to praise of a particular thing he does: he welcomes and supports travelling gospel workers who went out for the Name and took nothing from outsiders. This movement gives the letter its practical heart, showing what walking in the truth looks like in action.
section.thesis: Hospitality to gospel workers is not a minor courtesy but partnership in the truth: by supporting those who go out for the Name, Gaius becomes a fellow worker in their mission.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Gaius's faithful welcome of strangers; sending them on worthily because they went out for the Name; and the call to support such workers as fellow workers for the truth.

verses.text: Beloved, you are {{pistos|faithful}} in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are {{xenos|strangers}} to you.
They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner {{axios|worthy}} of God.

units.label: Partners in the mission
units.note: for the Name they went out

verses.text: For they went out on behalf of the {{onoma|Name}}, accepting nothing from the Gentiles.
Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be {{synergos|fellow workers}} for the truth.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy, reliable. It describes someone who can be counted on to do what is right, again and again. Gaius is commended not for a single grand act but for a faithful pattern of caring for the brothers, especially those he had never met.

xenos.gloss: A stranger or foreigner; the root behind the New Testament word for hospitality, which literally means love of strangers. The point is striking: Gaius served brothers who were strangers to him, welcoming them for the sake of Christ rather than because of prior friendship.

axios.gloss: In a manner worthy of, fitting to. To send the workers on their way worthy of God means to provide for them generously and honourably, as a right reflection of the God they serve, not with grudging or minimal help.

onoma.gloss: Name. On behalf of the Name means for the sake of Jesus; the Name stands for His person and honour. The workers travelled for Christ's sake and refused pagan support, so the church must be the ones to sustain them.

synergos.gloss: A fellow worker, co-labourer. By supporting the travelling teachers, those who stay home become genuine partners in the same mission. Hospitality and giving are not spectator kindness; they make the giver a true colleague in the work of the truth.

basic.context: Now the elder praises something specific: Gaius has been opening his home to travelling gospel workers, even ones he had never met. These men went out to preach for Jesus and refused to take money from unbelievers, so it fell to fellow Christians to support them. The elder says that when Gaius helps them, he becomes a partner in their mission.
basic.hermeneutics: This is warm, practical instruction, not a rigid rule about house guests. The abiding principle is clear and still binding: God's people should generously support those who give their lives to the gospel, and by doing so they share in the work itself. Hospitality here is mission, not just manners.
basic.originalLanguages: Gaius is faithful, pistos, reliable over time. The men are strangers, xenos, the very word behind hospitality, which means love of strangers. He is to send them on worthy, axios, of God. They went out for the Name, onoma, that is, for Jesus. And those who support them become synergos, fellow workers, in the truth.
basic.typology: The travelling workers who go out for the Name, taking nothing from outsiders, follow the pattern Jesus set when He sent out His disciples to depend on the welcome of God's people. Gaius's open home is a small picture of the whole church as a place of welcome for Christ's messengers.
basic.christ: The workers went out for the Name, the name of Jesus. Christ Himself had nowhere to lay His head and sent His followers to rely on hospitality. To welcome His messengers is, in His own words, to welcome Him. Supporting the mission is a way of serving Christ directly.
basic.god: God is honoured when His people care generously for gospel workers, sending them on their way in a manner worthy of God Himself. He notices faithful, quiet service to strangers and counts it as partnership in His mission.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus said welcoming His messengers is welcoming Him. Paul teaches that those who preach the gospel should live by the gospel. And Hebrews urges believers not to neglect hospitality to strangers.
basic.oneStory: God's plan to reach the nations runs through sent workers and the people who support them. Gaius's open door is a thread in that great story: ordinary believers making the mission possible, becoming fellow workers for the truth that is spreading to the world.

context.literary:
Verses 5 to 8 are the first body section of the letter, and they run in a clear sequence: a commendation, a request, a reason and a conclusion. The commendation comes in verses 5 and 6a, the request in verse 6b, the reason in verse 7, and the conclusion in verse 8, which opens with "therefore." The elder argues as he praises. Gaius is told what he has done so that he will see why it deserves to continue.

The unit is held together by a play on the idea of going. The brothers "went out" in verse 7, and Gaius is to "send them on their way" in verse 6. The home church receives, and the travellers move on. The passage thus pictures a chain: a church that sends, workers who go, and a household that takes them in along the road. Gaius is one link.

Verse 6 begins as report and ends as a request. Its first half tells Gaius what has been said of him, and its second half asks him to do it again. The little phrase "you will do well" is a polite formula, the sort of thing a friend writes when making a request he expects to be granted. It is courtesy with a firm edge.

Verse 8 changes from "you" to "we." Until now the elder has spoken to Gaius about Gaius, and here he draws himself and the whole circle of believers into the duty: we ought to support such men. The shift widens the application, so that what was praise for one person becomes a standard for all. The unit ends on a purpose clause, "so that we may be fellow workers," which is the point the whole passage was moving toward.
context.historical:
Travel in the first century was slow and dangerous, and lodging was a problem. Public inns were often noisy, costly and unsafe, so travellers with any connections stayed with acquaintances, and a letter of introduction could open a door. Christians took this practice and made it a mark of their faith. Paul's letters assume it constantly: he expects a church to help him on his way, Romans 15:24 and 1 Corinthians 16:6, he commends Phoebe so that she will be welcomed, Romans 16:1-2, and he tells Titus to equip Zenas and Apollos for the road, Titus 3:13.

The verb the elder uses for sending the brothers on their way is the same one found in those passages, and it meant more than waving goodbye. It meant providing food, money, companions and whatever else the next stage of the journey needed. Gaius was being asked to fund the next leg.

The workers had "gone out for the Name" and accepted nothing from the Gentiles. In the ancient world, wandering teachers and philosophers often collected fees or gifts from their audiences. The brothers refused this, so that no one could say they preached for profit. It also meant that they relied wholly on believers. The Didache, an early Christian manual, later gave rules for receiving such travellers, which shows how common and how open to abuse the arrangement became.

The pressure behind the letter is real. A church could easily decide to turn away unknown teachers, either from caution about false teachers, which 2 John 10 and 1 John 4:1 take seriously, or from jealousy of its own authority. The balance between welcome and discernment is a live concern here, and Gaius needs to hold both. The brothers he receives are not strangers in the sense of unknown outsiders. They are people who went out for the Name and whose character is attested by many.
context.canonical:
The principle that those who give themselves to proclaiming the gospel should be supported by those who receive it is rooted in the Old Testament. The Levites had no land and lived from the offerings of the people, Numbers 18:21-24, and Paul appeals to the same logic, along with the command not to muzzle an ox, in 1 Corinthians 9:9-14. He concludes that the Lord commanded those who preach the gospel to live from the gospel. Galatians 6:6 and 1 Timothy 5:17-18 say the same from other angles.

Jesus gave the pattern in the sending of the Twelve and the seventy-two. They were to take no bag and no money and to stay in the house that welcomed them, because the worker is worthy of his wages, Matthew 10:8-10 and Luke 10:7. He added that whoever receives a messenger receives Him, Matthew 10:40-42, and He will say on the last day, "I was a stranger and you took Me in," Matthew 25:35. Hospitality to Christ's people is hospitality to Christ.

Hebrews 13:2 and Romans 12:13 make hospitality a standing duty of every believer, and elders are to be hospitable, Titus 1:8. Second John 10 and 11 qualify the welcome by forbidding it to those who do not bring Christ's teaching, so that the same pair of letters teaches both open doors and watchful ones. Third John supplies the open-door half, and Diotrephes will show the opposite failure.

The "Name" is a New Testament shorthand for Jesus. The apostles rejoiced to be counted worthy of suffering "for the Name," Acts 5:41, and Paul was told how much he would suffer for His name, Acts 9:16. The workers of Third John belong to that line.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants Gaius to see his hospitality as part of the gospel mission and not as a private kindness. He does this in three moves. He praises what Gaius has done, which is a form of encouragement. He asks him to carry on and to do it generously, "in a manner worthy of God." And he gives the reason, which is that the workers went out for the Name and that those who help them become partners.

The argument is directed at a believer who may have been wavering. Diotrephes is about to be named as the man who shuts the door, and the elder knows that Gaius will feel pressure to follow suit or at least to keep quiet. By describing hospitality as a share in the work of the truth, the elder gives Gaius a reason to hold his ground that goes beyond politeness: refusing the brothers would mean withdrawing from the work itself.

The first hearers were meant to understand that supporting missionaries is not an optional extra for the specially generous. The elder says "we ought," which is the language of debt and duty. The whole church is meant to see itself as part of the sending.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage records a specific arrangement: itinerant workers, a church that received them, and a rule of not taking support from outsiders. It does not command every Christian to take strangers into their home in every circumstance, and it does not say how a church should structure its missionary funding. What carried over is the principle. Those who give their lives to proclaiming Christ should be supported by the people who benefit, and supporting them is a real share in their work.

The verses also prescribe a standard of care: to send people on "in a manner worthy of God." That asks for generosity that matches God's character and not for the minimum. We should apply this with wisdom. The same New Testament that urges hospitality also warns against welcoming those who deny Christ, 2 John 10, so the passage does not turn into a duty to fund anyone who arrives. It describes how a healthy church treats genuine workers, and it asks us to ask the same question: who is doing the work of the truth near us, and how can we help them go on?

debates.question: Who are the 'Gentiles' from whom the workers took nothing?

views.label: Unbelievers, the pagan public
views.case: The word translated Gentiles is the same one Jesus uses of non-believing outsiders in Matthew 5:47 and 6:7, and many take it here to mean the unconverted. The workers refused payment from those they preached to, as Paul sometimes did, 1 Corinthians 9:12 and 2 Corinthians 11:7, so that the gospel would not look like a commercial offer.

views.label: Gentile converts
views.case: A smaller group reads the word as non-Jewish believers who might have offered help. On this view the workers refused even this, relying only on the home churches. The text itself gives no sign that the persons are converts, and the word is not normally used that way.

views.label: Outsiders in general, whatever their background
views.case: Others take the word broadly as everyone outside the believing community, whether Jewish or not, so that the point is simply that the workers did not live from the wider public.

debates.bearing: The first reading best fits the wording. In every case, the result is the same: the support of the brothers rested on fellow Christians, which is why Gaius's help mattered so much.

debates.question: What does 'fellow workers for the truth' mean?

views.label: Fellow workers with the truth
views.case: The Greek noun for fellow worker is followed by a dative that can be read as 'with the truth,' as though the truth itself were a partner in the work. This reading draws on the personification of the truth in verse 12, where the truth testifies for Demetrius.

views.label: Fellow workers for the truth
views.case: Most translations, including the BSB, take the dative as one of advantage: they work on behalf of the truth. This fits the use of the word elsewhere, where fellow workers serve the gospel, as in Romans 16:3 and 2 Corinthians 8:23.

views.label: Fellow workers with the brothers, in the truth
views.case: A third reading hears the word as 'fellow workers with them,' joined to the travelling workers, and sees the truth as the sphere in which they work together. Support is a partnership between those who go and those who send.

debates.bearing: The wording is slightly open, but all the readings agree on the main point: the supporter and the missionary share a single work, and the truth is the cause that unites them.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 5 begins with a phrase that is better rendered "you do a faithful thing" than simply "you are faithful." The elder uses pistos with the verb poieo, so he is describing an action that expresses faithfulness, and then says "whatever you work" for the brothers, using the verb ergazomai, "to labour." The language is of work done reliably, not of sentiment. The "brothers" are the fellow believers who came to him, and the added "and especially strangers" uses xenos, the word that is the first half of philoxenia, "love of strangers," translated hospitality in Romans 12:13 and Hebrews 13:2. The elder never uses the noun here, but its shape is in the verse.

The verb for sending in verse 6 is propempo, "to send forward." It is a travel word, and the passages in which it appears show what it meant: the church at Antioch "sent on their way" Paul and Barnabas, Acts 15:3, and Paul hopes the Romans will "equip" him for his journey, Romans 15:24, with the same verb. It carries the idea of an escort and supplies, so Gaius is asked to do more than say farewell.

The adverb in "worthy of God" is axios, "in a manner worthy," used by Paul of walking worthily of the calling, Ephesians 4:1, or of the Lord, Colossians 1:10, and, in Romans 16:2, of receiving Phoebe "in a manner worthy of the saints." The standard is God Himself. It echoes the standard Paul sets for how believers walk.

In verse 7 the elder says they went out "for the sake of the Name," using the article and no further explanation. This is an absolute use. The Name is a recognised shorthand for Jesus, and Acts 5:41 provides the closest parallel: the apostles rejoiced to suffer shame "for the Name." The word for "Gentiles," ethnikoi, is used in Matthew of pagans and outsiders, which supports the view that the workers refused money from non-Christians.

Verse 8 contains the word synergos, "fellow worker," a favourite of Paul, who uses it of Prisca and Aquila, Romans 16:3, and of Titus, 2 Corinthians 8:23. The elder applies the title to supporters, not only to the travellers, so that giving counts as working. The verb the BSB renders "support" carries the sense of welcoming and taking someone up, so the duty includes both receiving the workers and underwriting their journey.

typology.type: The workers who go out for the Name
typology.fulfillment: The brothers who go out dependent on others' welcome echo Christ's own pattern and His instructions to the Twelve and the seventy-two, Matthew 10:8-10 and Luke 10:1-7. The correspondence is complete in Christ, who Himself had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58, and who was sent by the Father, John 20:21. The escalation is that these workers go out in His name and by His authority, not their own. The type falls short because they are imperfect messengers, and the supply they depend on is sometimes denied, as the next verses show.

Gaius shares in the work by hosting those who do it. This anticipates Christ's teaching that a cup of cold water given to a disciple will not lose its reward, Matthew 10:42, and that kindness to His people is kindness to Him, Matthew 25:35-40. The escalation comes at the final judgment, when the Lord will publicly acknowledge what was done in secret. The type falls short because Gaius's service is partial and local, while the reward promised is given by Christ's grace and not as wages, Romans 6:23.

typology.type: Sending on their way worthily of God
typology.fulfillment: The church's sending of its workers points to the Father who sends the Son and the Son who sends the church, John 20:21, and to the Spirit who sets people apart and sends them, Acts 13:2-3. The escalation is that human sending takes part in a divine sending that began before the church existed. The type falls short because human senders can fail to send, as Diotrephes does in the next verses, while God never abandons the mission.

study.christ:
The Name for which these workers go out is the name of Jesus, and the way they travel is shaped by His own pattern. When He sent out the Twelve and then the seventy-two He told them to take no bag and to rely on the house that welcomed them, Luke 10:4-7. He Himself had no place to lay His head, Luke 9:58, and women supported His ministry out of their means, Luke 8:3. The workers of the third letter walk the road that He walked.

The passage also shows how Christ identifies with His messengers. He said that whoever receives a disciple receives Him, and whoever receives Him receives the One who sent Him, Matthew 10:40. A cup of cold water given to one of His followers will not lose its reward, Matthew 10:42. In the great judgment scene He will say that what was done for the least of His brothers was done for Him, Matthew 25:35-40. So the home that opens its door to the brothers has opened it to Christ, and Gaius's love, which the travellers reported to the church, is love for Him.

The verses also turn our attention to the nature of Christ's mission. He came as a stranger into a world that did not receive Him, John 1:11, and He was refused a welcome in some places, Luke 9:53. Those who bear His name meet the same range of responses: welcome in one house and refusal in another. The elder's contrast between Gaius and Diotrephes is a small version of the world's response to Christ.

Finally, the phrase "fellow workers" has a Christological root. Jesus said that the Father is still working and that He is working too, John 5:17, and in the Great Commission He promised to be with His workers to the end of the age, Matthew 28:20. Those who help the mission are joining a work that is first of all His, and the support they give is part of that larger work. We should not make Gaius a symbol of Christ. The point is that the Christ who was sent, welcomed by some and rejected by others, stands behind every messenger and every host.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who works through partnership. He could advance the gospel without human help, but He has chosen to do it by sending workers and by supplying them through the generosity of others. The elder can speak of "fellow workers" because God has made the supporter and the missionary co-labourers in one task. That does not make God dependent on His people. It shows how generously He shares His work and His credit.

It also shows that God cares about the manner of service, not only the result. The workers are to be sent in a manner "worthy of God." That phrase suggests a standard drawn from God's own character: lavish, unhurried, caring for the traveller's need. A grudging gift or a hasty handshake would fall short of it. The way we treat the people who serve Him is a statement about how we think of Him. Paul uses the same standard when he asks the Romans to welcome Phoebe worthily of the saints, Romans 16:2.

The passage also shows that God notices what is done in quiet. The elder knows about Gaius's care of strangers because others carried the news, but behind that stands the One who sees what is done in secret, Matthew 6:4, and who does not forget the work and love shown for His name, Hebrews 6:10. Hospitality that no one else sees is seen by Him.

We can see a tension the passage holds together. The workers refuse payment from outsiders, so that the gospel is free, yet the church is told to support them, so that the workers are not left without provision. God's grace is freely offered, Matthew 10:8, and still He builds a body that carries the costs. Freedom and cost are not at odds.

This shapes worship. We honour God not only in song but in the practical help we give to those who carry His message, and in the welcome we give to strangers. When we host or send or give, we do something that God counts as service to Himself.

crossReferences.note: Jesus says that whoever welcomes a messenger of His welcomes Him and the Father who sent Him, and that even a cup of cold water will not lose its reward. This is the root of the elder's confidence that hospitality is a share in the work.

The seventy-two are told to stay in the house that welcomes them, eating and drinking what is offered, because the worker is worthy of his wages. The travelling workers of Third John live under this instruction and depend on homes like Gaius's.

The Lord prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel. Paul sometimes chose not to use this right, but he insists on it as a principle, which is the principle the elder applies in verse 8.

The apostles rejoiced to be counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name. This is the closest use of the absolute 'the Name' in the New Testament, and it shows that the phrase named Jesus and carried the willingness to suffer for Him.

Paul asks the church to welcome Phoebe in a manner worthy of the saints and to help her with whatever she needs. The wording of 'worthy' and the practical help match the elder's request in verse 6, showing a common early Christian way of speaking.

Titus is told to equip Zenas and Apollos so that they have all they need. The verb for sending on their way appears in the same sense of supplying travellers, which shows what Gaius is being asked to do in verse 6.

The same elder forbids welcoming anyone who does not bring the teaching of Christ, since greeting such a person shares in his evil deeds. Together the two letters show that hospitality is a duty directed by truth, and that welcome and discernment belong together.

Believers are not to neglect hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it. It gives the standing duty that lies behind Gaius's habit and treats the stranger as someone who may carry more than he seems.
On the last day the King says, 'I was a stranger and you took Me in.' It is the deepest reason for the elder's praise: welcoming the stranger who belongs to Christ is received by Christ Himself.

Paul calls Prisca and Aquila his fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their lives for him. It shows that 'fellow worker' was Paul's title for those who shared his labours in practical ways, not only for fellow preachers.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God has made a people to be a blessing to others. He told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and the story of Israel is the story of that blessing narrowing and then widening again. Abraham himself is remembered as the man who welcomed three strangers at his tent and fed them, Genesis 18:1-8, and the law told Israel to love the foreigner because they had been foreigners in Egypt, Deuteronomy 10:19. The pattern of a welcoming household in a world of wanderers was written into God's people from the start.

In Christ the blessing reaches the nations, and the church is sent out to carry it. The book of Acts is a story of people going out and people receiving them, from the church at Antioch laying hands on Barnabas and Saul to the households that opened their doors along the road, Acts 13:2-3 and 16:15. Third John is a small letter from the same movement, and Gaius is one of those hosts. The workers go out, as Jesus said they would, for the Name, and the church's welcome decides how far the message travels.

This is how the great story advances at ground level: not only through famous preachers but through the ordinary people who feed them, house them and send them on. The elder is clear that these supporters are co-workers in the truth. The story does not tell of the mission without them.

It also looks ahead. The mission is moving toward a day when people from every nation will stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and the One who was a stranger in His own world will welcome His people into His Father's house, John 14:2. The hospitality of Gaius belongs to the age between, when welcome is given to messengers on the road. In the new creation the road ends and the welcome is complete: God will dwell with them, Revelation 21:3. Every open door on the way is a foretaste of that home.

sermon.title: Walk in the Truth, Part Two
sermon.why: In this second message on 3 John, Begg treats Gaius's hospitality and generosity, showing how supporting gospel workers makes believers fellow workers for the truth. A faithful, practical exposition of this movement.

quiz.q: Why does supporting the travelling workers matter so much?

options.text: By supporting them, believers become fellow workers for the truth, sharing in the mission itself.
options.note: Verse 8 makes support a genuine partnership in the work of the gospel.

options.text: Because hospitality is a nice thing to do for guests.
options.note: It is kind, but the deeper point is real partnership in mission, not mere courtesy.

options.text: Because the workers would otherwise be lonely on the road.
options.note: Companionship helps, but the issue is sustaining the gospel mission.

options.text: Because it earns the giver a good reputation.
options.note: The motive is the Name of Christ and the truth, not personal reputation.

quiz.q: What is striking about the people Gaius served?

options.text: They were strangers to him, welcomed for Christ's sake rather than because they were friends.
options.note: Verse 5 stresses that he served brothers who were strangers, the heart of true hospitality.

options.text: They were fellow believers, the brothers, in genuine need of help.
options.note: True, but the striking detail is that they were strangers to him, not merely brothers.

options.text: They were local church members he already knew well.
options.note: They were travelling workers, strangers to Gaius, not familiar locals.

options.text: They were wealthy patrons who repaid him.
options.note: They took nothing from outsiders; they depended on the church's support.

quiz.q: Why did the workers accept nothing from the Gentiles?

options.text: So the gospel would be free and its support would rest on God's people.
options.note: Refusing pagan money kept the message free and placed the duty on the church, verses 7 and 8.

options.text: So they would not appear to be preaching the gospel for money.
options.note: A real part of it: guarding the gospel's credibility, though the elder's stress is that the church must support them.

options.text: Because they had taken a vow of poverty.
options.note: The text does not mention a vow; the concern is the gospel's credibility and the church's part.

options.text: Because Gentiles had no money to give.
options.note: It was a deliberate principle, not a lack of available funds.

quiz.q: What does sending them on their way worthy of God mean?

options.text: Providing generously and honourably, in a way that reflects the God they serve.
options.note: Worthy of God calls for open-handed, fitting support, verse 6.

options.text: Equipping them well with provisions for the next stage of the journey.
options.note: This captures the practical sense of send on their way, though worthy of God adds the honouring motive.

options.text: Giving them the bare minimum to get by.
options.note: The standard is worthy of God, which rules out grudging or minimal help.

options.text: Sending them away as quickly as possible.
options.note: The aim is generous support, the opposite of hurrying them off.

questions: Gaius welcomed and supported strangers for the sake of Christ. Who are the gospel workers in your life, and how could you support them more generously?
The elder says supporting such workers makes us fellow workers for the truth. Do you see your giving and hospitality as real partnership in mission, or as an optional extra?
True hospitality here means love of strangers, not just of friends. Where is God calling you to open your home, table, or resources to someone you do not yet know?
The workers refused to depend on outsiders so the gospel would stay free. How can you help keep the good news freely offered in your own setting?
This positive picture of Gaius stands right before the warning about Diotrephes. When it comes to welcoming others, which of the two are you more like this season?

translationNotes.note: The phrase for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you, highlights hospitality, philoxenia, which literally means love of strangers.
Send them on their way, propempo, was a near technical term for equipping travellers with provisions, money, and companions for the next stage of the journey.
The Name stands for Jesus; going out for the Name means for His sake. The Gentiles here are unbelieving outsiders from whom the workers would take no support.
